claims.text: Machine-learning interatomic potentials can achieve accuracy near that of their underlying DFT calculations for multicomponent metallic systems.
A moment tensor potential offers a favorable balance between accuracy and computational cost.
An ML-IAP can be trained on elemental and binary free-energy data and then refined by transfer learning for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Training data spanning elemental, binary, ternary, and quaternary Nb-Ta-Mo-W systems can be used to construct a potential for quaternary MoNbTaW.
The proposed transferred ML-IAP can reproduce solid and liquid fusion free energies for CoCrFeNi, AlCoCrFeNi, or similar multicomponent alloys.
The ML-IAP will retain vibrational, anharmonic, and electron-vibration contributions to fusion free energy.
HEA free-energy models can contain static, vibrational, electronic, and configurational contributions.
The ML potential encodes local bonding environments and vibrational modes that mediate free-energy contributions in both solids and liquids.
The ML potential directly captures electron-vibration coupling effects.
Transfer learning allows interpolation from well-characterized elemental and binary systems to complex multicomponent HEAs.
Enhanced-sampling molecular dynamics captures the necessary solid-to-liquid free-energy pathways and thereby preserves fidelity.
The proposed method will achieve free-energy errors of only a few meV per atom relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed method will reduce computational cost by at least an order of magnitude relative to explicit AIMD.
The proposed method will significantly outperform TOR-TILD for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
The method is expected to apply to metallic alloys from binary through quinary compositions within about 100 K of their melting points.
Explicit AIMD and, where available, TOR-TILD calculations under identical composition and temperature conditions provide the reference benchmark.
The hypothesis is falsified if free-energy MAE exceeds approximately 10 meV per atom, melting temperature error exceeds approximately 100 K, or cost reduction is less than tenfold.
